# Hatthipālajātaka (Ja 509)

**ID:** Ja 509
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Hatthipālajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul14.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Hatthipālajātaka* (Ja 509) is a birth story set at Jetavana illustrating the theme of the Great Renunciation (*mahānekkhamma*), recounting how the Bodhisatta previously abandoned royal worldly life [Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative, the childless king Esukārī and his royal chaplain agree that any sons born to them will share the kingdom; the chaplain and his wife (in the epilogue identified as Mahākassapa and Bhaddā Kapilānī) bear four sons who are future great disciples: the Bodhisatta (Hatthipāla), followed by brothers identified as Anuruddha, Mahāmoggallāna, and Sāriputta [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Fausböll 1887]. Though appointed heir to the throne, Hatthipāla renounces worldly power to pursue the ascetic life, soon inspiring his three brothers, his parents, and ultimately the king and queen (identified with the Bodhisatta’s parents Suddhodana and Mahāmāyā) to follow him into homelessness [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Fausböll 1887]. The story also includes an episode in which a tree deity is threatened with destruction when its tree is marked for felling [Schmithausen 2009].

 Confirming these verse parallels, DharmaNexus records internal Pali matches between Ja 509 (§24.3–26.2) and SN 1.4 and SN 2.27, in addition to extensive parallels in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and the Tibetan *Damamūko-nāma-sūtra* [DharmaNexus].

The text exercised significant influence across Theravāda literature and practice. The arrangement of its forest hermitage, magically constructed by Vissakamma, became a standard literary template referenced elsewhere in the Jātaka commentary [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities; Fausböll 1891]. In Myanmar, the fifteenth-century monk-poet Raṭṭhasāra composed a well-known poetical version of the Jātaka [Ray 1946], while modern Burmese teachers frequently cite Hatthipāla's spontaneous attainment of jhāna upon looking at the Ganges as evidence of matured past perfection (*pāramī*) [Pa Auk Sayadaw, Light of Wisdom; Ledi Sayadaw 2007]. In seventeenth-century Sri Lanka, the story inspired the Sinhala poetic work *Atpalda* [Holt 1996].

- Resembling parallels: SN 1.4 Accentisutta; G3-Dhp 31–40 Gāndhārī 3rd Dharmapada Verses 31–40; G3-Dhp 41–50 Gāndhārī 3rd Dharmapada Verses 41–50; SN 2.27 Nandasutta
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Catuttho bhāgo) (Atk S0513a4) (§21.3–26.4 ↔ §5181–5194); Devaputta Saṁyutta (SN 2) (§24.3–26.2 ↔ §27.1.1–27.3.2); Devatā Saṁyutta (SN 1) (§24.3–26.2 ↔ §4.1.2–4.3.2)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): Saṅghabhedavastu 1 (SA_K01_vinv171u) [sa]; འཛངས་བླུན་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ། ([damamūko-nāma-sūtra]) (D0341) [bo]
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel matching engine — Supplied machine text-reuse alignments with SN 1, SN 2, Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Saṅghabhedavastu, and the Tibetan Damamūko-nāma-sūtra.
- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Provided opening commentary, character names (Esukārī), dialogue details, and samodhāna identifications.
- [Fausböll 1891] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka together with its Commentary, Vol. 5 (1891) — Showed cross-references in other Jātaka commentaries to the hermitage layout established in the Hatthipālajātaka.
- [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Provided narrative details regarding the renunciation of the four brothers and their parents.
- [Schmithausen 2009] Lambert Schmithausen, Plants in Early Buddhism and the Far Eastern Idea of the Buddha-Nature of Grasses and Trees (2009) — Noted the episode concerning the tree deity threatened with destruction.
- [Olivelle, Ascetic withdrawal] Patrick Olivelle, Ascetic Withdrawal or Social Engagement — Discussed the parallel father-son dialogue in the Mahābhārata, Uttarādhyayana Sūtra, and Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
- [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities] Steven Collins, Nirvana and Other Buddhist Felicities (1998) — Noted the forest hermitage motif and its comparison with the Mūgapakkha Jātaka.
- [Ray 1946] Niharranjan Ray, An Introduction to the Study of Theravāda Buddhism in Burma (1946) — Noted Raṭṭhasāra's 15th-century Burmese poetic composition of the Hatthipālajātaka.
- [Pa Auk Sayadaw, Light of Wisdom] Pa-Auk Sayadaw, Light of Wisdom: Meditation in Pa-Auk Forest Monastery — Documented modern Burmese Dhamma talks referencing Hatthipāla attaining jhāna upon viewing the Ganges.
- [Ledi Sayadaw 2007] Ledi Sayadaw, The Requisites of Enlightenment: Bodhipakkhiya Dīpanī (2007) — Cited Hatthipāla as an exemplar of the resolve (*chanda* and *viriya*) to renounce royal luxury.
- [Holt 1996] John Clifford Holt, The Religious World of Kīrti Śrī: Buddhism, Art, and Politics in Late Medieval Sri Lanka (1996) — Noted the 17th-century Sinhala poetic adaptation Atpalda based on the Jātaka.
